title: Trump and former fixer Michael Cohen bury the hatchet
summary: The president and his former fixer put their contentious past behind them and reunited on Cohen’s radio show after years of legal feuds and name calling.
story: President Donald Trump and his former fixer Michael Cohen are putting their contentious past behind them.

Trump on Thursday joined Cohen, who has testified against him in Congress and in court, for an interview on Cohen’s radio show. The appearance, via phone, marked a new chapter in the pair’s fraught relationship after years of feuding that included Cohen’s serving as a star witness in two trials targeting Trump and congressional testimony in which he called his former boss a “racist, a con man and a cheat.”
During the show, Cohen struck a different tone, quoting a Bible verse about forgiveness, playing the song “Why Can’t We Be Friends?” and largely avoiding mention of their previous clashes.
Trump, for his part, touched on some of their past, saying his former ally had been “weaponized ... like nobody’s ever been weaponized.”

“They weaponized a lot of people, and I respect the fact that you recanted everything you said,” Trump told Cohen, who was sentenced to three years in prison for what he described in 2018 as actions done in “blind loyalty” to Trump.
Asked earlier in the day on CNN whether he was taking back anything he has said about Trump, Cohen responded, “What was said is said, and that’s where I stand with it.”
Cohen toed a similar line on his radio show, saying he did not want his fight with Trump to be the defining chapter of his life.

“The good memories don’t cease to exist simply because terrible ones followed them,” Cohen said. “True loyalty doesn’t mean pretending that you were never hurt. Reconciliation doesn’t mean surrendering your principles or rewriting facts. It simply means deciding that your story doesn’t have to end in its worst chapter.”
Trump’s remarks, however, were more reminiscent of his campaign-style rallies. He spoke in positive terms about the Iran war, disparaged Democrats and boasted about his economic policies.
The full interview is expected to air at 5 p.m. ET Sunday on Cohen’s WABC radio show, “When You Know, You Know.”
Cohen told NBC News before the interview aired Thursday: “There are things that he said to me that I have never heard before. It was a great interview, and people will be shocked when they hear it.”
The prospect of Trump’s joining Cohen for an interview would have been unthinkable until recently after Cohen cooperated with prosecutions of Trump.

For over a decade, Cohen worked for Trump as a devoted lawyer and fixer, and he famously said he’d “take a bullet” for his boss. They fell out in 2018, after Cohen was caught in the crosshairs of dual investigations by special counsel Robert Mueller and a U.S. attorney’s office in New York.

Cohen pleaded guilty that year to what a federal judge later described as a “veritable smorgasbord” of criminal conduct, including making secret payments to women who claimed they had affairs with Trump, lying to Congress about Trump’s business dealings with Russia and failing to report millions of dollars in income. That led to his three-year prison sentence.
“My weakness can be characterized as a blind loyalty to Donald Trump,” he said at his sentencing, adding that “time and time again I felt it was my duty to cover up his dirty deeds.”

Trump denied wrongdoing and claimed Cohen was lashing out only because he didn’t get a pardon. Cohen told CNN on Thursday before the radio interview aired that he didn’t ask Trump for a pardon during their conversation.

In 2019, Cohen testified before Congress about Trump’s business practices the previous year, telling lawmakers that “Mr. Trump inflated his total assets when it served his purposes” and “deflated his assets to reduce his real estate taxes.”

Those claims led New York Attorney General Letitia James to open an investigation into the Trump Organization soon afterward, while the Manhattan district attorney’s office began looking into Cohen’s claims that Trump had directed him to make hush money payments to adult film star Stormy Daniels.
Cohen testified at both trials, which separately led to a civil judgment of hundreds of millions of dollars against Trump’s company and a guilty verdict on 34 counts of falsifying business records.

Trump in 2023 filed a $500 million lawsuit against him, alleging he violated their attorney-client relationship by revealing privileged information. Trump dropped the suit later that year, shortly before he was scheduled to be deposed in the case.
Their public relationship took a turn in January, when Cohen claimed on Substack that he’d been “coerced” into testifying at the trials.

“I felt pressured and coerced to only provide information and testimony that would satisfy the government’s desire to build the cases against and secure a judgment and convictions against President Trump,” he wrote.
The district attorney’s and attorney general’s offices have said their investigations weren’t politically motivated.

Trump’s attorneys are now using Cohen’s comments in court filings for their pending appeals of his criminal conviction and civil judgment. The attorney general’s office shrugged off the effort in a March court filing.

“Whatever can be gleaned from this unsworn post, it is certainly not that Cohen gave false information to OAG during his interviews,” the filing said, noting that Cohen said on an ABC podcast in March that “[i]n no way, shape or form should it connote that the information that I provided [to OAG] was anything but truthful and accurate.”

Cohen confirmed to NBC News last month the New York Times’ report that he had had two in-person meetings with Trump since last year, one at his Bedminster, New Jersey, estate last year and then again at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida this year. He said the meeting was “warm and reminiscent of old times.”
Cohen said Thursday on Substack that his interview with Trump was based on “forgiveness.”
At the end of their on-air conversation Thursday, Cohen quoted the 1978 Peaches & Herb song “Reunited” as it played in the background, telling listeners: “Yeah, reunited, and it feels so good.”

title: This is the dorm registry I wish I had as a college freshman
summary: A dorm registry can help you pull together everything you need for college — including bedding, supplies and more — and give friends and family an easy way to help.
story: When I moved into my college dorm as a freshman,  I remember wishing there was a simple way to send friends and family a list of everything I still needed — similar to the registries people create for weddings and baby showers. Between bedding, storage, laundry supplies, toiletries and all the little things I didn’t realize I’d need until move-in day, the shopping added up quickly. I wanted a way to make a cohesive list that everyone could shop while avoiding bad communication that resulted in duplicates and deficits.

Since then, I’ve led the back-to-school shopping for my family. I handled my own college shopping and helped my brother, who’s now a senior in college, with his move in. Next up is my sister, who’s a senior in high school, and I’m already thinking about what she’ll need when it’s her turn to move into a dorm. This time, though, I’m making a registry.

A dorm registry can serve two purposes: It keeps your college shopping organized in one place, and it gives friends and family who want to support you an easy way to buy something you’ll actually use. Most if not all retailers keep track of what requests have been fulfilled so there won’t be any duplicate purchases and, depending on the retailer, you may also be able to have items shipped or picked up at a store near your college, which can be particularly helpful if you’re moving far from home or need to fly to school.

As someone who worked for her campus Residential Life office throughout all four years of college and helped support countless move ins and move outs, I know which dorm essentials students actually use (and which ones they probably don’t need). So below, I’ve rounded up places where you can create a dorm registry or shareable wishlist, along with the essentials I’d recommend adding before move-in day.

Where can you make a dorm registry?

Not every retailer offers a dedicated dorm registry, but that doesn’t mean you can’t make one. Many stores offer shareable wishlists that accomplish essentially the same thing: You can add the dorm essentials you need, send the list to friends and family and keep everything organized in one place. Below are the retailers I recommend for creating a dorm registry or wishlist, including options that offer shipping or pickup near campus.Note that all these retailers require an account, but the wishlist creation tools are free.
Amazon

Why I like it for college: Amazon is probably one of the easiest options for a dorm registry because you can put a wide variety of dorm essentials (bedding, storage, school supplies, tech accessories, toiletries and more) in one place. You can also assign priorities to items, which I like for distinguishing between the things you need before move-in and the things that would simply be nice to have.

Amazon doesn’t have a registry specifically for dorm rooms, but you can create a Gift List or Wish List and use it like one. To make a Gift List, go to Amazon’s Registry & Gifting page, select “Create” and choose the occasion you’re celebrating; you can also create a List through “Account & Lists” or directly from a product page. Once it’s set up, add dorm essentials as you shop.

How friends and family shop it: You can make an Amazon Gift List public and searchable or keep it shareable and send the link directly to who you want to have it. Amazon also tracks purchases, which helps prevent loved ones from buying the same items.

Shipping/pickup: You can assign a shipping address to an Amazon List, which makes this particularly useful if you want gifts sent to the address you’ll use while at college or mail room once your mailing ID is assigned. Items can be sent directly to your home address which is nice if you want to have safely, securely packaged boxes ready to go for move-in day.
Target

Why I like it for college: Target has nearly everything you might need for a dorm, but its large store footprint is what makes it particularly convenient. If you’re attending college away from home, you can shop before you leave and potentially pick up things closer to school instead of packing every pillow, storage bin and bottle of detergent into the car. Target has almost 2,000 locations across the U.S.

Target is one of my favorite options for this because it actually offers a College Wish List specifically designed for school planning. You can create one on Target.com  or in the Target app, then add products online or by scanning items in a Target store. Target also offers college-focused checklists to help you figure out what you might be missing.

How friends and family shop it: You can send friends and family a direct link — including a customized URL — or make your list searchable on target.com and in Target stores. When someone buys an item directly through the list, Target updates it to help keep track of what’s already been purchased.

Shipping/pickup: This is where I think Target really shines for college students. Gifts can be shipped to the address attached to your list, and shoppers can also purchase registry and wishlist items online for order pickup. Target also offers drive-up pickup and same day delivery, depending on the order and location.
Walmart

Why I like it for college: Walmart is especially useful for the less exciting dorm purchases that are just as important as your bedding and decor — think cleaning products, toiletries, laundry supplies, snacks and class supplies. Its pickup option also makes it useful for replenishing essentials once you’re already on campus.

For dorm shopping, I’d recommend creating a Walmart Wishlist. Walmart says its former “Any Occasion” registries are now wishlists, which can be created on walmart.com or in the Walmart app by going to lists under the “My Items” tab, and then “Create a Wishlist.” You can add products online, through the app or even in store by scanning a product’s barcode.

How friends and family shop it: Once you’ve created your wishlist, you can share it via a copied URL, email or social media. Unlike Walmart’s traditional gift registries, wishlists aren’t searchable by friends and family, so you’ll need to send them the link. Gift givers can purchase products, mark them as purchased and have eligible items shipped directly to you.

Shipping/pickup: Walmart offers both shipping and local pickup/delivery services, although fulfillment options depend on the product and location. For pickup orders, you select a local store and time slot and Walmart notifies you when the order is ready.
Dormify

Why I like it for college: Dormify takes a lot of the guesswork out of college shopping because you aren’t sorting through products intended for an entire house. The site is centered on dorm-friendly categories and features an extensive checklist for students that helps structure shopping plan — including twin XL bedding, storage and organization, bath and laundry, lighting and no-nails decor — so it’s a particularly good option for first-year students furnishing their space for the first time.

Unlike most of the retailers on this list, Dormify is specifically focused on college living and has a dedicated Dorm Wishlist. You can create and manage your wishlist through Dormify’s site and add items from its assortment of twin XL bedding, storage, bath and laundry products, seating, decor, lighting and other dorm essentials.

How friends and family shop it: Dormify has a “Find a Wishlist” tool that lets friends and family search using the student’s name, with optional filters, including state. That means relatives don’t necessarily have to keep track of your individual wishlist link to find it.

Shipping/pickup: Dormify also advertises a Pick Up Near Campus program, which is particularly helpful if you had to drive far or fly to school. Dormify does not have standalone brick-and-mortar stores but you can have items shipped to partner retailers by your school, such as Williams Sonoma, Pottery Barn, or West Elm.
MyRegistry.com

Why I like it for college: College students rarely buy everything from one store. A universal registry lets you make one master dorm list without limiting yourself to a single retailer’s inventory. You can also sync existing registries from other retailers into MyRegistry.

MyRegistry is different from most other options on this list because it isn’t a retailer — it’s a universal registry platform. You create a free account and can then use its browser tool or mobile app to add products to one registry from virtually any online retailer. That means your Target sheets, Amazon desk lamp and highlighters from Walmart don’t need to live on three separate lists.

How friends and family shop it: Instead of sending everyone multiple wishlist links, you share one MyRegistry link. When someone chooses an item, they’re directed to the original retailer to complete the purchase. MyRegistry tracks purchased items on the universal list to help prevent duplicates.

Shipping/pickup: It’s important to note that MyRegistry doesn’t fulfill the order itself. Because shoppers ultimately purchase through the retailer that sells the item, shipping, delivery and pickup options are determined by that retailer.
Pottery Barn Teen

Why I like it for college: PB Teen is particularly useful if you want to make your dorm feel more put together while still shopping for practical necessities. Its dorm assortment covers everything from mattress toppers and twin XL bedding to under-bed storage, laundry supplies, shower caddies and desk accessories, so you can build most of your room from one wishlist. I also like that its site has dedicated dorm-shopping tools, including a dorm checklist and Build Your Bed tool, which can be helpful for first-year students who aren’t sure where to start.

Pottery Barn Teen has a dedicated Dorm Wishlist, making it one of the most college-specific options on this list. You can create a wishlist online and add products from PB Teen’s Dorm Shop, which includes twin XL bedding, storage and organization, bath and laundry essentials, lighting, desk accessories and decor.

How friends and family shop it: Once your Dorm Wishlist is set up, friends and family can search for it on PB Teen’s website using your first and last name, with optional filters for your state, birth month and year. PB Teen also lets you manage your list online and link a wishlist that was originally created in one of its stores.

Shipping/pickup: This is one of the biggest reasons I like PB Teen for college students: The retailer has a Pick Up Near Campus program and lets shoppers filter dorm products based on whether they’re eligible for the service. PB Teen also promotes the option to ship orders to a store, which can help you avoid packing bulky dorm purchases and transporting them from home. Availability varies by product and location, so I’d check what’s eligible near your school before placing an order.
Crate & Barrel

Why I like it for college: I see Crate & Barrel as less of an “everything you need for freshman year” option and more useful for higher-quality items that can follow you beyond the dorm. Think bedding, bath essentials, organizers or kitchenware you’ll eventually use in an apartment. Group gifting is also useful for pricier items.

Crate & Barrel doesn’t have a college-specific registry, but it does allow registries for occasions beyond weddings, including housewarmings — consider dorm room shopping like a mini-housewarming. It is an option for someone furnishing their first space. You can create and edit a registry online or through the Crate & Barrel app and add items digitally or with help from an associate in the store.

How friends and family shop it: Friends and family can search for a registry and purchase directly from it, and Crate & Barrel keeps track of purchased gifts. It also offers group gifting, which lets multiple people contribute toward certain higher-priced registry items.
Shipping/pickup: Eligible registry purchases of $49 or more ship free, according to Crate & Barrel.
The Container Store

Why I like it for college: Storage space is one of the biggest challenges in a dorm room, and organization is where The Container Store really stands out. Its dorm checklist includes under-bed storage, bed risers, desktop organizers, hampers, shower caddies, hanging closet organizers, over-the-door storage and stacking drawers — basically the products that help you make use of every inch of a small room. The retailer even recommends choosing free store pickup at a location near campus in its dorm-shopping materials.

The Container Store doesn’t have a college-specific registry, but you can create a Wish List and use it as a dorm registry. You can name your list — something as simple as “[Your Name]’s College Dorm” works — and add the storage and organization products you want to it. The retailer specifically says its wishlists can be used for occasions like graduations and shared with family and friends.

How friends and family shop it: Once you’ve made your list, The Container Store lets you send it via email to friends and family so they can shop from it. Unlike PB Teen’s Dorm Wishlist, however, this isn’t a full-fledged college registry program; it’s better thought of as a shareable wishlist that you can adapt for dorm shopping.

Shipping/pickup: The Container Store offers free in-store and curbside pickup for online orders. You select the store at checkout, and the retailer sends an email or text when the order is ready. That makes it especially helpful if there’s a Container Store near your college: Instead of filling your car with bulky bins, drawers and organizers, you can order online and pick them up closer to campus. Local delivery is also available in select markets.

How to shop for dorm essentials

Shopping for a dorm is different from shopping for a bedroom at home: You’re working with limited space, may be sharing that space with someone else and will likely have to move everything again at the end of the school year. Before you start adding items to your dorm registry or wishlist, these are the factors you should consider.

Set a budget before you start shopping and prioritize necessities over decor and convenience items. Bedding, bath essentials, laundry supplies and a few storage solutions are worth budgeting for first; you can always buy additional organizers, decorations and accessories after you’ve moved in and know what you actually need.

You also don’t need to buy everything new. If you already own towels, hangers, a desk lamp or other items that work for your dorm, bring them rather than replacing them simply because you’re going to college. A registry can also be a good place for more expensive essentials that friends or family may want to contribute to.

Check your school’s housing website for your residence hall’s floor plan, room dimensions and a list of included furniture before buying larger dorm items. Knowing the size of your bed, what’s already provided and how much floor and closet space you’ll have can prevent you from buying things that won’t fit.

I recommend waiting until move-in to buy some organizers for this reason. It’s much easier to determine whether you need another rolling cart or set of drawers once you unpack and can actually see the space you’re working with.

Read your college’s residence hall policies before buying appliances, furniture or anything that attaches to the walls or doors. Schools can have specific rules about items like microwaves, mini fridges, coffee makers, extension cords, candles and wall-mounted products, and your school may already provide some of the larger items you’re considering.
Don’t forget about your actual dorm room door, either. Check rules and measurements before buying over-the-door organizers, hooks and similar products, since door dimensions and policies can vary.

Coordinate with your roommate before buying anything you only need one of, such as a rug, vacuum, trash can or other shared supplies. Decide who will bring each item rather than splitting the cost of everything, if possible — it’ll make figuring out who takes what at the end of the year much easier.

I’d also avoid relying on your roommate for personal essentials you’ll use frequently. Sharing a vacuum is one thing; having to track down your roommate every time you need laundry pods or utensils is another.

Before buying something, consider how frequently you’ll use it and whether your college already gives you access to one. Many campuses have resources like printers and other school supplies in libraries, computer labs or residence halls, so you may not need your own version of everything.

For inexpensive items you’ll use constantly, having your own may still be worth the convenience. But if something is expensive, bulky and only useful a few times a semester, check what’s available on campus first.

Prioritize durability for products you expect to use throughout college, especially items that will be packed, unpacked and transported repeatedly. Hampers, storage bins, luggage and organizers can take a beating during move-ins and move-outs, so spending a little more on sturdy versions may make sense if you plan to use them for several years.
For inexpensive items you don’t expect to keep after college, durability may matter less. Think about the item’s expected lifespan before deciding where it’s worth spending more.

Think about where everything will go when you move out before buying bulky furniture, storage or decor. If you’re flying home, live far from campus or don’t have much storage space at home, you’ll need to either transport your belongings, pay to store them near school, sell or donate them or replace them the following year.
Collapsible, stackable and multipurpose products can be especially useful for this reason. The less space something takes up when you’re not using it, the easier your end-of-year move will be.

Wait on nonessential storage, decor and convenience products if you’re unsure whether they’ll fit or whether you’ll actually use them. Moving in with the basics and shopping for the rest afterward can save you money and keep you from overcrowding your room.

This is also where ordering for pickup near campus can come in handy. Instead of transporting every possible item from home, you can make a list of things you may need and order eligible products once you’ve seen your room and figured out what’s missing.
Frequently asked questions

A dorm registry is a shareable list of items you need for your college dorm room. It works similarly to a wedding or baby registry, allowing friends and family to see what you need and, depending on the retailer, which items have already been purchased.

Not necessarily, but a shareable wishlist can work essentially the same as a dorm registry. Some retailers offer dedicated college registries or dorm wishlists, while others let you create and share a general wishlist with friends and family.

You can start making a dorm registry once you know where you’ll be living and what your college provides or allows in its residence halls. Starting early also gives you time to compare prices and coordinate larger purchases with your roommate.

Yes, you can make dorm registries or wishlists at multiple retailers. You can share each list separately or use a universal registry service, like MyRegistry.com, to combine products from multiple stores into one list.

You should buy the essentials you’ll need immediately, including bedding, toiletries, towels, laundry supplies and basic organization products. You can wait to buy some storage, decor and other nonessential items until you’ve seen your room and know how much space you actually have.

Don’t add appliances, furniture or other large items until you’ve checked your college’s residence hall rules and what your room already includes. Schools may prohibit certain appliances and often provide items like a desk, chair, dresser or mini fridge.

You might. A dorm registry or wishlist can be useful for returning college students who need to replace or upgrade their essentials. It can also be helpful for someone moving into a different type of housing or whose needs have changed.
Why trust NBC Selected?

I am the editorial operations associate for NBC Selected. For this article, I did extensive research and pulled from my years of experience with back-to-school shopping and working in residence life to give you the most practical, helpful recommendations for how to create a dorm registry and what to put on it.

title: No cable? No problem — here’s where to stream this season’s Premier League matches
summary: Here’s everything you need to know about the 2026-27 Premier League season, including when it starts, how to stream, who’s playing and more.
story: Soccer fans, your time is now — it’s officially almost Premier League season. The English Premier League is one of the best and biggest soccer leagues in the world, drawing over half a million American viewers per match during the previous season.

Whether you’re a longtime Prem veteran or a newly-minted fan who wants to keep up with your World Cup faves, you’re in the right place. Below, I’ve gathered everything you need to know about this upcoming Premier League season, including key dates and where you can stream everything live.
When is the 2026-27 Premier League season?

The 2026-27 Premier League season officially kicks off Friday, August 21 with a match between the reigning champions (and my favorite squad) Arsenal, at home against newcomers Coventry City. The season runs through the final matchday on May 30, 2027, with each of the 20 teams playing 38 matches (19 home and 19 away) for a grand total of 380 matches.
For a full match schedule, check the Premier League website, where you can find dates, times and locations, along with league standings, team and player stats and more.
How to watch the 2026-27 Premier League season
Peacock Premium

Peacock is the official streaming broadcast partner of the Premier League in the US, with matches available to be livestreamed in real-time. You can also stream full replays of all available matches shortly after each livestream ends, along with Spanish-language matches via Telemundo’s broadcasts. Peacock Select, the streaming service’s basic tier, costs $8.99 per month, but doesn’t include access to sports, movies or Peacock originals. However, Peacock Premium, which costs $12.99 per month, includes Premier league games, along with all shows, movies and sporting events with ads, while Peacock Premium Plus, the ad-free tier, also includes downloads and goes for $16.99 per month or $169.99 annually.
Disclosure: Peacock is the streaming service of NBC News parent company NBCUniversal; NBCU is owned by Comcast, which is a co-owner of Hulu.
FuboTV Sports

Fubo’s monthly Sports package is available for as little as $31.40 per month, and includes over 70 channels, some of which will be streaming Premier League matches in 4K. The package also includes access to other popular leagues like Germany’s Bundesliga, France’s Ligue 1, and the North American international league, CONCACAF.

title: Surrogate who had baby against parents’ wishes denies ‘political theater’ accusation
summary: McKenna West, the surrogate in the center of a multi-state legal battle over a baby who was born with a rare heart condition, sought to “set the record straight.”
story: The surrogate at the center of a multistate legal battle over a baby who was born with a rare heart condition sought to “set the record straight” about her motivations in an op-ed published in the New York Post on Thursday.

McKenna West, a cardiac nurse from Alaska, gave birth in Texas last week to a baby boy whom she was carrying on behalf of Omar Ahmed and Nausheen Gilkar. The baby, Rumi, had surgery Monday for a rare congenital heart condition, hypoplastic left heart syndrome, which often requires lifelong medical care.
In her editorial, West said she knew from her experience as a nurse that the baby she was carrying had a chance at survival through surgery.
“People have called this political theater. It isn’t,” she wrote. “This is about giving an innocent child a shot at the life he deserves.”
A representative for Gilkar and Ahmed declined to comment on West’s editorial in a statement to NBC News on Thursday, citing a request from the court-appointed guardian in the legal proceedings.

“The Guardian Ad Litem appointed to this case at the request of McKenna West and the Texas Attorney General has urged the parties to refrain from making statements to the press in the interest of protecting the privacy and well-being of the child,” the statement said.

Relations between the couple and West were contentious in the months leading up to his birth after the baby was diagnosed during a 20-week anatomy scan in April, according to court documents both parties filed in Alaska this summer.
The surrogacy agreement that West signed before an embryo transfer last year included a clause that the parents could ask West to have an abortion in case of fetal abnormalities, the documents said.

West chose not to pursue a scheduled appointment to terminate the pregnancy after the heart defect was discovered, saying she worried she would “not be able to live with” herself, according to her legal complaint seeking custody in Alaska.
West contends in the court documents that after she refused to have an abortion, Ahmed and Gilkar tried to pressure her with legal threats over the surrogacy agreement she signed.

A counterclaim the couple filed last month said that they initially communicated to West that she was in breach of their contract but that they later sent messages that said they understood her refusal.
The next several weeks would begin a legal battle that spanned three states.

According to court documents in Alaska, the biological parents sought an order in California establishing them as the baby’s parents after West severed contact with them in May. West then sued in Alaska in June to try to stop the California proceedings and asked an Alaska judge to give her custody of the baby.

The couple, based in California, filed a counterclaim in July alleging that they wanted the California order to begin setting up medical care for the baby, since West refused the abortion and refused to provide updates on the baby’s health. They also asked the Alaska court to award them $100,000 in damages, the counterclaim said. West filed a motion to dismiss the counterclaims this week.

While the couple was looking to get care for Rumi at Cedars Sinai Medical Center in Los Angeles, West sought consultation from doctors in Texas. She wrote in her editorial Thursday that the hospital had excellent outcomes for the operation Rumi would need and that she had friends in the area.

“The contracting couple wanted me to deliver the baby at a hospital in California, but that hospital didn’t have the same perfect track record of success, and I had no one to support me there,” she wrote.

West has alleged in her editorial and in court documents that Rumi’s parents have refused to commit to provide him with lifesaving care, a claim the couple has denied. Court documents in the California case are sealed, but their filings in Alaska emphasize that the parents “never said they would refuse medical treatment as recommended by a doctor for their son.”

The allegation was repeated by Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who asked a court to order doctors to treat the baby with the required surgery. The court appointed a guardian to receive all “pertinent medical information” about the baby after his birth.

The couple’s attorney previously said in a statement that the couple were focused on their baby’s health and that they are devastated to have their “family tragedy transformed into political theater.”

West has been represented by the Alliance Defending Freedom, a conservative legal organization that advertises that it was involved in overturning Roe v. Wade, and the case is being championed by Paxton, an anti-abortion Republican who is also a candidate for the U.S. Senate. The case has become a political proxy fight over abortion, but West said Thursday that she is not trying to take someone else’s baby.
She said she feels the baby needs an advocate “as he gets the ongoing treatment his fragile heart requires.”
Rumi underwent a complex palliative heart operation Monday called a Norwood procedure, which is the first of three procedures in the treatment for his heart condition.
West said in a statement Thursday that she was glad to hear Rumi was recovering from the surgery.
“My focus has always been on protecting this precious baby’s life,” she said.

The procedure’s in-hospital survival rate is 90%, but the five-year survival rate ranges from 60% to 75%, according to the Cleveland Clinic. There is significant risk involved in the operations to treat hypoplastic left heart syndrome, Dr. Scott Hadland, the chief of adolescent and young adult medicine at Mass General Brigham for Children and Harvard Medical School, has told NBC News.
“A lot of kids don’t survive from one surgery to the next, and there can be a lot of impairment in terms of normal healthy development,” he said.

title: FBI thwarts an alleged ISIS-inspired plot to bomb New York Capitol
summary: Jessica Bowie, 35, is accused of telling a confidential source with the FBI that she supported ISIS and asking for help learning to make explosives.
story: A woman has been charged with providing support to a terrorist group after she was accused of plotting an ISIS-inspired attack on the New York Capitol in Albany, federal officials said Thursday.

Jessica Bowie, 35, of Albany, is alleged to have told a confidential source that she supported the Islamic State militant group, commonly known as ISIS, and asked for help learning to make explosives, according to a criminal complaint filed in U.S. District Court for the Northern District of New York.
She was arrested Wednesday by the FBI’s Joint Terrorism Task Force in Albany, First Assistant U.S. Attorney John A. Sarcone told reporters Thursday.
Bowie is expected in court Thursday afternoon on a single charge of attempting to provide material support to a designated foreign terrorist organization.

According to the complaint, Bowie converted to Islam five years ago, became radicalized online and created several social media accounts using an honorific Islamic name. She appeared to have created multiple accounts, because they were “frequently suspended by providers for violating their terms of use,” the complaint says.
Several accounts alleged to trace back to Bowie posted messages expressing support for terrorism from May to July.

Bowie swore her allegiance to ISIS in multiple audio recordings in English and Arabic, and she once wrote, “Praise be to Allah for September 11,” Craig Tremaroli, the special agent in charge of the FBI’s Albany field office, said at a news conference Thursday.
The complaint alleges that Bowie communicated from July 16 through Aug. 17 with a confidential source who was working with the FBI and posing as an ISIS facilitator.

She told the source that she wanted help to carry out an attack on the New York Capitol, according to the complaint. The building was less than 2 miles from her home, and she said she wanted to do something to “harm the enemies of god,” the complaint says.

The complaint alleges that Bowie visited the Capitol five times from July 21 to Aug. 9 and that surveillance teams observed her photographing the area. She is alleged to have said in messages to the source that she wanted to have an “affect on the American system.”
“I want to destroy as much of the building as possible and kill the senators while they are meeting,” a message included in the complaint said.

Two other confidential sources met with Bowie in Albany this month in a meeting that was recorded, the complaint says. Bowie is alleged to have said she wanted to attack the building on a day when the most senators would be present.
She hoped to escape after the attack and, if she evaded the authorities, planned to return for future plots, the complaint says.

“Miss Bowie didn’t just want to kill lawmakers; she wanted a complete disruption of our government. And after that, she planned to flee the country and one day come back to ‘do more,’ such as New Year’s Eve in Times Square, even stating she would come back to attack the White House and the president,” Tremaroli said.
Asked why she wanted to target the state Capitol, Bowie is alleged to have said, “Ideally it would be the White House with the president, but like, that’s an even harder job.”
She was also asked whether it would bother her if other people, including Muslims, died in the attack, the complaint says.

“I’d say it definitely bothers me, and I know I’m going to hear about the things after — what’s going to bother me, especially if there’s a Muslim, if there’s children, pregnant women,” Bowie responded, according to the complaint.
She went on to say, however, that she hoped Allah would forgive her, it says.

One of the confidential sources gave Bowie $200 to purchase bomb-making materials, which she is alleged to have done Aug. 5 at a Home Depot. She then gave the items to the confidential sources when she met with them in the days that followed, authorities say.
The complaint alleges that Bowie asked one of the sources last week about obtaining a handgun, saying she wanted the weapon “so if the cops do get towards me during the operation I can shoot back.”
She met with the confidential sources to buy a gun and ammunition Wednesday, according to the complaint.
Tremaroli said the investigation started over a month ago.

Sarcone said: “I want the American people to know this: Today’s announcement will have a chilling effect on anyone in this country who is being radicalized or considering acts of violence and on our enemies whose governments support death to America. We are vigilant, we are prepared, and just as we stop this defendant, we will continue to disrupt plots and protect the American people.”
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said in a statement Thursday she is “grateful” to the FBI and the New York State Police.

“Earlier this year, amid a rise in political violence and threats against public officials, we took steps to strengthen security at the State Capitol and across state government,” she said. “While there is no immediate threat at this time, we will continue working closely with our law enforcement partners to protect New Yorkers and keep our communities safe.”
The charge against Bowie carries a statutory maximum prison term of 20 years, up to a $250,000 fine and a lifetime term of supervised release.

title: Who Is Chanty Beluga? Meet the Comedian Behind the Unforgettable Name
summary: Who is Chanty Beluga? What to know about the viral meme, created by comedian Courtney O’Donnell, of a woman introducing herself over and over again.
story: She’s going to a restaurant. She’s ordering takeout. She’s getting in an Uber.
In every instance, she makes sure to drop her name: Chanty Beluga.
Who is this smiling, millennial blonde woman whose videos have gone viral on TikTok? And where did that hypnotic and unique name come from?
Here’s what to know.
Who Is Chanty Beluga?
The character is the alter ego of comedian and actor Courtney O’Donnell, who posts TikTok videos of herself as Chanty Beluga.

Cheerful and demurely dressed, Chanty Beluga is always finding herself in situations where she has to use her goofy name. She’s checking in at a restaurant, ordering takeout, and introducing herself at a pool party.

The videos are quick and simple. Just a woman casually saying her ridiculous name, which seems to roll off the tongue and promote repeat listening. The character has already spawned multiple fan accounts on TikTok.

“This is so dumb and I see myself becoming rapidly obsessed with it,” one follower commented on a TikTok video of Chanty at a coffee shop. “No notes. Just a woman named Chanty Beluga in situations where she makes her name known.”
“Classic Chanty,” another one wrote.
“I would die for Chanty Beluga,” another commented.
Who Is Courtney O’Donnell, the Inventor of Chanty Beluga?

O’Donnell is a Los Angeles-based comedian who has a separate TikTok account under her real name. She posts short comedy skits as different, non-Chanty Beluga characters, from the host of the fictional “Yup, She Went There” podcast to a divorcée singing through the heartbreak.
She posted her first Chanty Beluga video on July 28 introducing herself, and it was a hit with nearly 500,000 views.

O’Donnell told Rolling Stone that she came up with the catchy name in the middle of the night while filming the upcoming comedy “Stephanie, Bride to Be” in Brooklyn, New York. She and the cast were “being silly” when it popped into her head.

“And I said, ‘Hi, my name’s Chanty,’ and we thought that was funny,” she said. “I was like, ‘Actually, my name is Chanty Beluga.’ We said the full name, and it seriously went viral in the room. We just could not stop saying Chanty Beluga. And I said, ‘Hi, my name’s Chanty,’ and we thought that was funny.”
Why Does the Internet Love Chanty Beluga?
The Chanty Beluga skits are so short, they allow O’Donnell’s followers to have fun by building out a longer story for the character.
“Chanty doesn’t play abt her takeout,” one follower commented on a video of Chanty Beluga ordering food.
“OMG IMAGINE BEING THE WORKER AND THE CHANTY BELUGA CALLS IN,” another joked.
The blank canvas of a character who’s not much beyond a funny name allows the internet to take it and run with it.

“She’s a Barbie doll. She’s a paper doll. You can put her in any situation. She can do anything,” O’Donnell told Rolling Stone. “I had this instinct to really build her up and create this crazy backstory, but I thought it was more interesting to allow the internet to create its own.”
Count Major League Baseball among those followers. The MLB X account posted on Aug. 18 that a woman named “Chanty Beluga” was presenting that day’s schedule of baseball games.

“Sometimes you go viral for something that you didn’t connect to, and I actually think this is really fun,” O’Donnell told USA Today. “I love pretending to be this woman on the internet who’s sort of quirky and basic and talking to people in the comments like I’m her.”
Then there’s one simple reason. Saying “Chanty Beluga” is fun.
“Something about the intonation of the words that feels like crack to say,” O’Donnell told Rolling Stone. “Something about the intonation of the words that feels like crack to say.”
Now the question is whether Chanty Beluga will reach the internet heights of 6-7 before people inevitably have had enough.

“I like the idea that she is the 6-7 for the girls and the gays,” O’Donnell told USA Today. “That would be really amazing. I don’t know. We’ll have to see. I’d be very happy. These things have a short shelf life, so I’m happy to just kind of be a part of it for now and let people have their fun. If we see some Halloween costumes, I won’t be mad.”

title: ‘I’m Not Hiding How Much This Hurts’: Malcolm-Jamal Warner’s Widow Honors His Birthday with an Emotional Message
summary: Malcolm-Jamal Warner’s widow honored the late “Cosby Show” star with a moving Instagram post on what would’ve been his 56th birthday on Aug. 18.
story: Malcolm-Jamal Warner’s widow honored the late “Cosby Show” star with a moving Instagram post on what would’ve been his 56th birthday on Aug. 18.
Tenisha Warner shared a picture of the couple’s 9-year-old daughter standing in a room filled with stuffed animals, while a “Happy Birthday” banner hung on a wall.

“Every year we spent his birthday at home, just the three of us,” Warner wrote. “He always said that was all he needed because it brought him the most joy to begin every new year of his life with us. The only other guests were our daughter’s dolls and stuffed animals. Every single one was lined up in the dining room to celebrate with him.
Warner also did not shy away from the agony she still feels about her husband’s death.
“Today is his birthday, and we are breaking as we try to learn how to be here without him,” she wrote.

“I’m not hiding how much this hurts. My gift to him includes my pain, because pain this deep only exists where love ran that deep. So today I’m sharing this with you who loved him too, the gift he gave us: he loved us with his whole heart, in ways I will never know again.”

Malcolm-Jamal Warner died July 2025 at the age of 54 in an accidental drowning while on vacation in Costa Rica with his wife and daughter. According to Costa Rica’s Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ), he died as a result of asphyxia by submersion.

In September 2025, Tenisha Warner made her first public comments about her husband’s death as their anniversary approached while also announcing the creation of the charities River & Ember and The Warner Family Foundation in his honor.
“I can still hear my husband’s laugh, still feel the way he made room for every part of me — every tear, every dream,” she wrote, in part, on Instagram.
“Together we carry the legacy my husband and I began— one that nurtures children’s inner light and gives young artists the freedom to create outside the lines,” she added.

In July, Tenisha Warner sued Malcolm-Jamal Warner’s mother, Pamela Warner, for breach of contract involving the couple’s prenuptial agreement, which she claims they signed eight days before marrying in 2022. The lawsuit says the actor did not fulfill the obligations of the prenup, while Tenisha Warner claims that he “agreed to purchase and maintain a term life insurance policy on his life in the amount of $1,000,000,” with her as the “sole beneficiary.”

However, she says he never bought the life insurance policy for him or for her, even though they had an agreement. Her complaint also says the actor agreed to pay her $16,000 a year on their anniversary, create a retirement account and pay her a salary of $5,000 per month as his “chief of staff” but never did so.
The complaint claims that Tenisha Warner is owed “no less than $1,276,042.46,” plus interest and attorney’s fees and cost.
Pamela Warner has also publicly mourned his death.

“Malcolm was an exceptional husband, father, and son — a man deeply in love with life, his wife and his daughter,” she wrote in a statement posted on Instagram in August 2025. “He was not only my son, but also my teacher, coach, confidant, business partner, and best friend. He was the son that his father was immensely proud of and loved fiercely and unconditionally.”

TODAY.com has reached out to Pamela Warner for comment. According to a statement she shared with USA Today, a settlement has been reached. The statement said claims that Pamela sought to prevent her granddaughter from receiving financial support are untrue.

title: Bunnie XO Calls Life Post-Divorce a ‘Blessing,’ Shares She Wants to Have a Baby
summary: Bunnie XO opened up about her plans for having a baby during her TODAY interview.
story: Bunnie XO called her post-divorce life “a blessing” and reiterated that she still wants to have a baby after splitting from ex-husband Jelly Roll earlier this year.

The bestselling author and host of the hit “Dumb Blonde” podcast spoke on TODAY with Jenna & Sheinelle Aug. 20 about what her life is like since Jelly Roll, whose real name is Jason DeFord, filed for divorce on May 18, according to court records from Williamson County, Tennessee.
The split came two months before what would’ve been the couple’s 10th wedding anniversary.

“I know when something like that that’s deeply personal happens, it’s a beautifully tragic, but at the same time there’s always a silver lining, there’s always something better to look forward to,” Bunnie, whose real name is Alisa DeFord, told Jenna Bush Hager and Sheinelle Jones. “There’s so much more to talk about with me especially, and with women, than their past lovers and people in their lives.”
On the June 18 episode of her “Dumb Blonde Podcast,” Bunnie XO confirmed the split. She also said it was “not mutual” and not her choice to break up.

She also revealed the surprising news that they still plan to have a baby together and would raise the child as co-parents. Jelly Roll has two children from previous relationships, daughter Bailee Ann, 18, and son Noah Buddy, 9.
Bunnie XO confirmed on TODAY that she still wants a child, but it was not clear if she wants the baby with her estranged husband.

“So I definitely still want to have a baby, and that’s going to be one of my newest chapters of my next book, and I can’t wait for you guys to read about it because it’s been one hell of a journey, let me tell you,” she said.

Bunnie XO and Jelly Roll have previously talked about their desire to have a child together. The couple announced in 2024 that they were trying to conceive through in vitro fertilization. Bunnie XO said on her June podcast episode that they had lost four embryos during their relationship together.
She also revealed on her podcast that Jelly Roll had started dating. In her interview on TODAY, Bunnie XO made it sound like she is also enjoying the single life herself.
“Ladies, they should’ve never let me back out in the streets because I love it here, and I’m never going back,” she said.

“I feel like us as women, we put ourselves aside so much for partners or friends, kids, and it’s like we don’t pour into ourselves, and sometimes you need to be selfish and you need to pour into yourself,” she continued. “And I just hope my journey can show people, ‘Hey, you know what, no matter how hard the situation you’re going through, you’re going get through that, you’re going to rise up, and you’re going to be an even better version of yourself.”
Jelly Roll cited irreconcilable differences as the reason for the split, according to the court filing. He and Bunnie XO each spoke out separately about the divorce filing.
Jenna and Sheinelle asked if Bunnie XO’s direct messages have been blowing up since the news of her divorce.
“I’m having the freaking time of my life,” she said. “I’m just thriving. I never thought it would turn out to be such a blessing, but it’s such a blessing, and I’m so thankful.”
She called her DMs “a freakin smorgasbord” of men and women.
“It’s so much fun in there, I don’t even know who to reply to,” she said. “It’s a lot. I love reading everbody’s DMs. Some of these pickup lines are amazing.”
Bunnie XO is also grateful if her perseverance through a difficult time in her personal life can help others.

“I’m not anybody’s role model, but if there’s something I can do that can encourage and inspire anybody along the way, then I hope that they get to take bits and pieces of my mistakes and my journey and apply it to their life,” she said.

title: Eli Rallo Reveals Cover, Excerpt from First Chapter of Her Debut Novel, ‘I Hope Eden Reads This’
summary: Eli Rallo reveals the cover and an excerpt from her debut novel, “I Hope Eden Reads This,” set to publish March 9, 2027.
story: It is a truth universally acknowledged that a good story starts with a good first line. In TODAY’s “Cold Open,” authors tease their buzzy upcoming release by revealing and explaining its first line, paragraph or page.

Writing about 20-something female friendships and platonic “breakups” for her 2025 essay collection “Does Anyone Else Feel This Way?” influencer and podcaster Eli Rallo knew she had more to say on the topic.
But she needed to go deeper.

“I didn’t want to do it in a nonfiction vertical. I feel like I’ve said all I needed to say about my own personal experience or my own advice,” Rallo, who rose to online fame for doling out lifestyle “rules” for women navigating quarter-life, tells TODAY.com. “I don’t think I really necessarily have a ton of advice about how to navigate this.”
“I more so wanted to put words to it to make people feel less alone about it,” Rallo, 28, adds.

The result is her first novel, an exploration of the specific heartbreak that comes with dissolution of a decadeslong friendship, titled “I Hope Eden Reads This” — and TODAY.com has an exclusive first look.
After announcing her fiction debut to her cumulative one-and-a-half million social media followers in September 2025, Rallo officially unveiled its cover on Aug. 20.

The cover is an artistic portrait of two young girls, one with her eyes closed, another staring down the viewer. Rallo says she wants it to feel “so sad and tender” but also “emotional and intimate.” (While this cover was always her favorite, an alternative option was shaping up to be the winner from her publisher — until she got a “lovely, serendipitous” email on her birthday confirming the final.)
From the jump, Rallo says she knew the book needed to be blue.
“I felt like it had a Taylor Swift, ‘1989’ thing going on, like beachy blue vibes, New York City, all of that,” Rallo says.

“I Hope Eden Reads This” follows two childhood best friends, Penelope and Eden. Its premise establishes that the two, for whom “the term ‘best friend’ has never been enough,” are no longer speaking, and Penelope is falling apart. The book is told in dual timelines — one chronicling their friendship history, the other showing the aftermath of the breakup. The story is purposefully only told from Penelope’s perspective.

“I felt like the story had to be told from one side. It really is Penelope’s story, and Eden has a perspective in my mind and in my heart,” she says. “I’ve already received so much feedback from beta readers that people want to know more about what Eden was thinking, and I would rather leave them with that desire and maybe revisit it.”
So it’s fitting that the book’s first line of the first chapter starts with “I,” as Penelope reflects on the preteen years of her friendship with Eden:
I taught Eden how to kiss. I taught Eden how to do most things, if the definition of ‘taught’ is being brave enough to try things first and then report back my often-measly findings.

The book officially begins with a prologue, which Rallo says she wants keep a surprise for readers. So for TODAY.com’s “Cold Open” she shares the first few paragraphs of Chapter 1 (read the excerpt in full below).

She says this section was the very first thing she wrote about Eden and Penelope. Rallo wanted to channel “preteen awkwardness” and foreshadow an undercurrent of “toxicity” in intense female friendships that can go unnoticed — that is, until the relationship’s gone.

“When I look at the two characters, they have such an interesting relationship where they rely on each other for different things, and I think that their reliances on each other wind up becoming their demise in certain ways,” she says.

She says the book is generally inspired by friendship loss, but “what happens to these girls has never happened to me.” Rather both characters are a “patchwork quilt” of “every woman I’ve ever gotten to know or love,” she says. Excited to see whom readers will relate more with, she’s already prepared a Buzzfeed-style quiz to determine if you’re more of an Eden or more of a Penelope — and had to add an 11th question because she initially tied for both. (Rallo’s a Penelope, by one.)
When she first started to pitch the book, Rallo says people opened up to her about their own friendship losses, stories they seemed to have never been able to share before.
“It really felt like, at least to me, that everybody had an Eden. Whether they were ... 21 and an intern or 60 and a senior editor, everybody had an Eden story to share,” she says.
“I Hope Eden Reads This” is Rallo’s third book, joining her essay collection and 2023’s modern dating advice tome, “I Didn’t Know I Needed This.”

“I my whole life wanted to be a fiction writer,” she says. “I think my first two books were the only first two books I ever could have written. But I would be lying if I said that this didn’t feel like the biggest homecoming for me.”
Read the Beginning of ‘I Hope Eden Reads This’ Chapter 1

I taught Eden how to kiss. I taught Eden how to do most things, if the definition of ‘taught’ is being brave enough to try things first and then report back my often-measly findings. I was kissed first. So, I taught Eden how to kiss. This is mostly because I sought kissing out, and then kissing sought me out in return.

I was kissed for the first time 6 months prior, by a boy with red hair and one skinned knee, while we were sitting on the swings at the park across the street from our school, our feet turned toward each other. His name was Henry. We did not do tongue. I reported back to Eden. It was quick and maybe lasted 3 seconds? I tried to count how long it lasted while we kissed. Because what was the point of being kissed if not to report every moment, every detail to my best friend? I had to memorize the choreography of the whole thing. Deliver the information to her like a birthday gift, wrapped with a bow, sparing no detail.

I was kissing half because I wanted to and half because I wanted to share a new bit of knowledge with Eden. I craved filling that role. The bold teacher. That tenacious 13- year-old girl. Always the first to raise her hand. Always the first to try. The only thing Eden ever did first was get her period. She pulled me into the bathroom stall in 7th grade in the middle of lunch to tell me. We were 12. I faced her on the toilet. Read her the instructions on the back of a tampon box. I helped her put in a tampon for the first time though I had never done so myself. In every other way though, in any other scenario, I was first. Perhaps I was not better; I was hardly ever better. But I was always first.

title: ‘Saved By the Bell’ Turns 37: Watch TODAY Go Behind the Scenes of the Iconic Show in 1992
summary: “Saved by the Bell” executive producer Peter Engel talked to TODAY in 1992 about why the show was such a hit.
story: Welcome inside the TODAY Vault, where we revisit memories from our show when celebrities and newsmakers started discourse, made us laugh or shaped our culture. This latest installment highlights the “Saved by the Bell” craze, and aired on July 24, 1992, by which time the show had cemented itself as a linchpin in NBC’s Saturday morning lineup.
On Saturday mornings in the 1990s, the alarm didn’t give out a warning, but teens knew they had to make it on time for one thing: “Saved by the Bell.”
The show, which premiered on Aug. 20, 1989, had become a full-blown phenomenon by the ‘90s, so much so that TODAY had to go to the set to see just what all the fuss was about.

The antics of Zack, Kelly, Slater, Jessie, Lisa and Screech have been well documented: The show helped redefine Saturday morning television and would lead to the short-lived primetime series “Saved by the Bell: The College Years,” as well as “Saved by the Bell: The New Class,” which followed and ran for seven seasons. “Saved by the Bell” is sacred to kids of the ‘90s, with a reboot released earlier this decade on Peacock.
‘Saved by the Bell’s’ Connection to TODAY
“Saved by the Bell” proved so influential, in fact, that it even had an impact on TODAY.
NBC decided to scrap Saturday morning cartoons altogether, adding other comedies like “California Dreams,” as well as a Saturday edition of TODAY in 1992.

Other live-action series, such as “Hang Time,” “City Guys,” “One World” and “Saved by the Bell: The New Class,” would eventually follow in the years to come in what would be known as NBC’s TNBC Saturday morning lineup.
Why Did ‘Saved by the Bell’ Shy Away From Serious Subject Matter?

“Saved by the Bell” executive producer Peter Engel said the show was “vilified” by critics for not being “on the cutting edge” by failing to address teen issues such as alcoholism, child abuse, divorce, sexual assault or teenage pregnancy.
“Those issues are very, very real and those problems are very, very prevalent, but not to the majority of teenagers,” he told TODAY.

“The majority of teenagers are not pregnant. The majority of teenagers are not having drinking problems. The majority of teenagers don’t have abusive parents,” he added. “We felt there were enough other shows in primetime dealing with these issues that we would deal with the issues that confront kids everyday.”

While the show did indeed have plots involving everything from aliens to a love detector, it didn’t completely shy away from serious subject matter: Fans will no doubt point to the classic episode in which Jessie gets hooked on caffeine pills, sparking perhaps the series’ most memorable line: “I’m so excited! I’m so excited! I’m so ... scared!”
What Made ‘Saved by the Bell’ a Hit?
The TODAY segment noted that the show was seen in 28 countries, dubbed into foreign languages. At the time, the cast was preparing to shoot a full-length movie for television.
“I’m convinced that one of the keys to success of this show is that our kids are playing their real ages,” Engel said. “They were really 14 playing 14, 15 playing 15, et cetera.”

“And the message is that these kids always ended up doing the right thing. No matter how they deviated or scammed or conned to get to a certain point, in the final analysis, they always did the right thing. They always made the right choice,” he concluded.

title: Tia Williams Shares Details About Her Next Book for the 1st Time
summary: Tia Williams opens up about her next book for the first time and shares details. She is writing a followup to A Love Song to Ricki Wilde.
story: Tia Williams stopped by Open Book with Jenna to share some book recommendations and some news about her own books.
The romance novelist, who published “The Missed Connection” earlier this year, shared details about her next novel for the first time.
“This is the first time I’ve ever saying this,” Williams said with a smile.
“We won’t air this. But we will,” Jenna replied cheekily.
Tia explained that her next novel will be a follow-up to “A Love Song for Ricki Wilde,” which came out in 2024.
“Ricki Wilde’s best friend, Tuesday Rowe, the disgraced child actress, is getting her own book,” Williams said.

“A Love Song for Rickie Wilde” is a romance novel infused with magic about a florist in Harlem who falls for a musician with an old-world charm. Turns out his vibe is because he is literally from the past: Ezra is a time-traveling emigré from the Harlem Renaissance.
Tuesday is Ricki’s friend and a former child star who, apparently, will go on her own love journey, though we’ll have to see whether it will also be infused with the supernatural.

This isn’t the first time Williams has continued the universe of one book into another. Audre, Eva’s daughter in Williams’ 2021 book “Seven Days in June,” stars in her 2025 YA novel “Audre & Bash Are Just Friends.”
Speaking to TODAY.com in 2024, Williams shared the philosophy that guides all of her romance novels.

“I love love. I believe in it. I believe in love at first sight, all of that. I’m a very romantic person. I romanticize life. How grim and sad is your life if you can’t mythologize it? Because life is hard. So I’ve always just tried to make a story out of everything. I don’t want things to be run of the mill. I want everything to be high stakes, more vivid than average: The most interesting people you’ve ever met, the funniest dialogue, the best sex, like ever. Because ultimately, this is a gift from me, to Black women. Whoever else loves it is fabulous. But that’s my first target, and so I want it to be a real fantasy,” she said.

title: DEA Joins Investigation Into Hayden Panettiere’s Death
summary: The Drug Enforcement Agency is joining local authorities in the investigation into Hayden Panettiere’s death.
story: The Drug Enforcement Agency has joined local authorities in the investigation into the death of actor Hayden Panettiere, a source familiar with the probe tells NBC News.

The DEA has multiple agents assigned to the case, the source says. It’s unclear what their role will be in an investigation being led by the Greenville City Police Department and Greenville County Coroner’s Office in South Carolina.

Typically DEA agents probe into how a victim obtained the drugs and whether any associates or medical professionals involved in securing the drugs broke the law, the source tells NBC News. It’s unknown at this time if there were drugs involved in her case. DEA agents joined Los Angeles police in probing the death of “Friends” star Matthew Perry in 2024 from a ketamine overdose, leading to multiple criminal convictions for those who sold ketamine to him.

Panettiere was found in cardiac arrest on Aug. 16 when emergency personnel responded to a 911 call at a residence where she had been temporarily staying in Greenville, according to a statement by the Greenville County Coroner’s Office. The 36-year-old “Nashville” and “Heroes” actor was declared dead at 2:32 p.m. after EMS workers were unable to resuscitate her.
Dispatch audio from the emergency response references a possible overdose, but no cause or manner of death has been given by authorities.

“The cause and manner of death remain pending further investigation and the completion of additional studies,” the coroner’s office said in the statement. “This investigation remains active and ongoing.”
The news of the DEA’s involvement comes after Panettiere’s mother, Lesley Vogel, told NBC News that a detective informer her a narcotics investigator is involved in the case.
“It leads me to believe they have questions,” Vogel said.
Vogel said Panettiere’s body has been returned to the family, and they are currently working on plans for a funeral service.
An autopsy completed on Aug. 17 did not find any signs of trauma that would have contributed to her death, according to the coroner’s office.

Brian Hickerson, who had an on-again, off-again relationship with Hayden Panettiere that included allegations of domestic violence, was at the scene when the actor was pronounced dead, according to a report issued on Aug. 18 by the Greenville City Police Department.
The department said on Aug. 19 that they performed an “unrelated” welfare check at Hickerson’s family home. Hickerson did not immediately respond to NBC News’ request for comment.

title: Meghan Markle, Prince Harry and Their Kids Are Moving Back to the UK
summary: Prince Harry and Meghan Markle, along with their two children, are set to move back to the United Kingdom.
story: Prince Harry and Meghan Markle are returning to the United Kingdom, a source familiar with the couple’s plans tells NBC News.
The couple, along with children Archie, 7, and Lilibet, 5, have been living in Montecito, California, since taking a step back from their royal duties in 2021.
King Charles III was first made aware of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex’s plans to move across the pond on Sunday, Aug. 16, the source says.

The news comes after the family visited with the king and Queen Camilla in July. The reunion marked the first time the British royals had seen their grandchildren in four years. According to The Telegraph, Harry and Meghan’s move was not discussed during the visit.
The source tells NBC News that the king welcomes the opportunity to see more of the Sussex family in a private and personal capacity.
As of now, Harry and Meghan will continue to be non-working royals and private individuals, the source says.
Additionally, another source close to the couple says the family is moving back to the U.K. for an “extended period” of time.

Over the summer, the Sussex family traveled to the U.K. for a number of public events, including the promotion of the 2027 Invictus Games. The king and queen then hosted them at Highgrove House, their private residence in Gloucestershire, England, on July 10, Buckingham Palace confirmed to NBC News.
Prior to this summer, the last time the king and queen saw Archie and Lilibet was in 2022 at Queen Elizabeth II’s Platinum Jubilee.
Since the family left the U.K., Harry has been attempting to repair his relationship with his father. In 2024, the king announced that he was diagnosed with an unspecified form of cancer.
In September of 2025, the father and son reunited for the first time after 19 months apart.

In a May 2025 BBC interview, Harry said he “would love reconciliation” with his family. “There’s no point in continuing to fight. Life is precious. I don’t know how much longer my father has. It would be nice to reconcile,” he added.
After the Sussex’s family trip over the summer, Meghan shared photos from their overseas holiday, including a visit to Princess Diana’s childhood home.

title: Nick Jonas Reveals He ‘Bombed’ His Audition For This Successful Disney Movie
summary: Nick Jonas reveals that he auditioned for a role in “Frozen” and “it went terrible.”
story: There could have been a world where Nick Jonas was part of a successful, winter-themed animated Disney movie — but he has since let it go.

The singer, along with brothers Joe and Kevin Jonas, chatted with “Frozen” stars Kristen Bell, Idina Menzel and Josh Gad during D23 for their “Hey Jonas!” podcast, where he revealed he “bombed” an audition for a role in the film.

“I auditioned for ‘Frozen,’” he said in the Aug. 18 episode, seemingly shocking the trio as he told them he read for the part of Kristoff, who is voiced by Jonathan Groff. “I went in and they said, ‘OK, what are you going to be singing today?’ I said, ‘Oh, I don’t know.’”

Stumping the person in charge of casting, Nick Jonas continued, “They’re like, ‘Do you have your sheet music?’ And I said, ‘No, no one told me I had (to bring it) ...’ and so I just said, ‘Can you play something from,’ I don’t know what I said, some musical theater song, and I bombed the audition. It was terrible.”
“What?!” Gad said, as Bell quipped, “That must have been why you didn’t get it.”
Gad jokingly added that Nick Jonas would have had “such better chemistry with Kristen than Groff.”
Nick Jonas agreed, saying that while he loves Groff, “I do think it would have been better to cast me.”
Kevin Jonas then questioned his brother’s team and why they didn’t properly prepare him for the audition.
“I’ve changed agencies three time since then,” Nick Jonas replied.
And despite not getting the role of the good-natured ice harvester, he said he and his family are “massive fans” of “Frozen.”
Back in May, Joe Jonas shared on their podcast that he too had a similar experience when he bombed his audition for “The Morning Show.”
After being put in “the saddest room you can imagine,” he recalled being able to hear the other actors auditioning for the same role. “And these guys were crushing it.”
“And I go in and I just crash and burn,” he said. “It was literally like, I don’t even know what I’m auditioning for ... It was just gone for me. And it was such a bad audition.”

title: See the Trailer for NBC’s New Drama ‘Line of Fire,’ Produced by Jenna Bush Hager
summary: A trailer for the new NBC drama “Line of Fire,” starring Peter Krause and Hope Davis and produced by Jenna Bush Hager, has been released.
story: Jenna Bush Hager is known for her work on daytime TV, but she’s about to make the move to nighttime.
A trailer for the new NBC drama “Line of Fire,” which is executive produced by the TODAY with Jenna & Sheinelle co-host, debuted exclusively on TODAY Aug. 20.

“A family of law enforcement agents bridges personal differences and crosses professional boundaries as they tackle cases for the FBI, US Marshals, Secret Service and Department of Justice,” reads NBC’s logline for the series, which was created, written, and showrun by Joshua Safran.

“After a seemingly cut-and-dry case turns into a deadly conspiracy, they must use the expertise from a lifetime of protecting civilians and politicians to protect one another and bring the killer to justice ... even if it means betraying their sworn code.”

Emmy nominees Peter Krause and Hope Davis star as a Secret Service agent husband and federal marshal wife, while Taylor Bloom, Kat Cunning and Tommy O’Brien play their kids, each in their own field of law enforcement.
The trailer weaves the complexities of family relationships with the challenge of working in law enforcement.

“Your whole family works in the field,” a man tells Bloom in the beginning of the trailer. “Two Secret Service Agents, a U.S. Marshal, a fed, and, now, a DOJ analyst. What your dinner table conversations must be like.”
“We’d have to have dinner together to know,” Bloom replies.
The trailer shows how the family interacts on various cases, balancing professional and personal affairs, before we see the group being told a killer was out to get one of them.
“How do you protect the world and the people you love in it at the same time?” Davis asks as the trailer ends.
After Carson Daly introduced the trailer on PopStart, Jenna shared that one of her former Secret Service agents served as a consultant for the series.
“I bet he’s got stories,” Savannah Guthrie said with a laugh.
“He’s got one or two,” Jenna responded.
Jenna spoke more about the series at the network’s Backlot Press Day Aug. 10 in Los Angeles.

“This is also about a family. I knew these people ... I had Secret Service men who would leave their family to protect mine,” she said. “So the dynamics of that are very much part of the DNA of what Josh has written.”
Krause, who previously starred on ABC’s first responder procedural “9-1-1” for eight seasons, called his newest project a “very interesting, unusual” show on TODAY in May.
“It’s a fantastic family-centered show, which is an action thriller, and the writer Josh Safran brings a lot of family dynamics to it —the good, the bad, the ugly, the funny, the sexy,” Krause said.
He also joked around about working with Jenna.
“You know, I’d be out there filming and I’d hear, ‘Again! Again! Faster, louder, funnier!’” he quipped.
“She’s been fantastic. Absolutely fantastic,” he added.
“Line of Fire” premieres Sept. 21 at 10 p.m. ET on NBC.

title: Sandra Bullock Details Late Partner’s Bryan Randall’s Battle With ALS For the First Time: ‘A Traumatic Diagnosis’
summary: Sandra Bullock is sharing how she cared for partner Bryan Randall in the final years of his life after his ALS diagnosis, and how his illness impacted their family.
story: Sandra Bullock is sharing how she cared for partner Bryan Randall in the final years of his life after his ALS diagnosis, and how his illness impacted their family.
The actor spoke in depth about Randall’s passing for the first time during an interview on the “Smartless” podcast, hosted by friends Jason Bateman, Sean Hayes and Will Arnett.
At the start of the latest episode, Bullock mentioned she had previously been a guest five years ago. But she said she “was not mentally there during that show.”

When Bateman asked what Bullock was dealing with during the time, she opened up about her relationship with Randall, who died in 2023 at the age of 57 following a “three-year battle with ALS,” his family shared at the time.
Later in the podcast, Hayes said Bullock confirmed to him before they started recording that she was finally ready to speak out. “I feel safe to talk to you guys about it,” she told the co-hosts.

“What I have now, I would not have to share had I not gone through that. I would not ever want to go through it again,” she said. “Though you never know, life ... it’s tricky. But I wasn’t allowed to speak about it. That was the request.”

She revealed that Randall asked her not to share his diagnosis with anyone, which “isolated” her throughout his treatment. She noted that he was diagnosed during the COVID-19 pandemic, further separating her from friends and family she could lean on.
Bullock said at that time she was also “panicking” as one of her two children, Louis and Laila, has “severe asthma” and she was trying to prevent them from contracting the virus.

The actor then discussed the process of Randall finding out he had ALS. She said he spent over a year completing different tests until doctors determined he had the disease, which affects the nervous system.

“His was not hereditary, which is, I think, a huge sigh of relief. But it was about a year and some of watching it to see what it is. It could have been this, could have been this. But what I saw, I knew. I knew it. And you have to quietly plan,” Bullock shared.

She said after caring for her father, who was ill, and her mother, who had cancer, she didn’t feel scared. But, she knew that she had to help her partner while also navigating being a mom to two young children, particularly daughter Laila, who viewed Randall “as a father figure.”
Eventually, Bullock told her sister about the diagnosis and she was the only other person who knew.

The actor recalled reaching out to different doctors to see if Randall could get on a list for trial drugs. She said she had “the privilege” of being able to pay for the caretakers that Randall needed.

“I think not talking for a while was good, and then when the physical illness was then coupled with the mental health aspect of things — it’s something that people don’t talk about, and it doesn’t happen to everybody — but it was a trifecta that was pretty dark. I had incredible nurses … they’re like four big brothers in my kitchen every morning,” she shared.
